title: Why Methods?
summary: Understand modularization: decomposing complex monolithic code into clean, reusable, independently testable functions.
learningOutcomes: Explain why breaking code into methods improves maintainability
Identify duplicated logic ready for extraction
Distinguish between standard library methods and user-defined methods

activities.title: Core Mechanics: Why Methods?

breakdown.whatIsIt: Comprehensive exploration of Why Methods? in Java.
breakdown.whyItMatters: Crucial for writing maintainable, reusable, and bug-free Java applications.
howItWorks: Decomposes complex logic into self-contained subprograms.
Allocates local variables on Call Stack frames.
Passes arguments by value, copying parameter data into frames.
Returns execution control back to caller upon reaching return statement.
keyTakeaways: Mastering Why Methods? is essential for Java placement interviews and clean architecture.
Methods enforce the DRY principle by eliminating redundant duplicate code.
Parameters act as local placeholders; arguments provide runtime values.
Always consider edge cases such as invalid input parameters or stack overflow.

activities.title: Verified Java Implementation: Why Methods?
activities.description: Notice how repeating discount logic three times clutters code, and how extracting it into a single method clarifies the program.

questions.prompt: What does the software engineering principle DRY stand for?
options: Data Recording Yield
Don't Repeat Yourself
Direct Return Yield
Dynamic Runtime Yield
questions.explanation: DRY stands for 'Don't Repeat Yourself'. It emphasizes extracting duplicate code into reusable components such as methods.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is NOT an advantage of modularizing code into methods?
options: Easier debugging and maintenance in a single place
Improved code readability and self-documentation
Guaranteed 100x execution speed increase by the CPU
Ability to unit test logic independently
questions.explanation: Methods improve organization, maintainability, and testability, but they do not automatically make code run 100x faster. Their primary advantage is human engineering quality.

questions.prompt: Which of these is an example of a built-in Java standard library method you have already used?
options: System.out.println()
Scanner.nextInt()
Math.max()
All of the above
questions.explanation: All three are built-in methods provided by standard Java packages (java.lang and java.util).

questions.prompt: What happens when a method is called in Java?
options: The program terminates immediately
Execution control transfers from the caller to the method, runs the method code, and returns back to the caller
Java creates a separate background thread without waiting
The method code is copied and pasted into the binary file at compile time
questions.explanation: When a method is invoked, program execution pauses at the call site, jumps to the method body, executes its statements, and then resumes right after the call site.

questions.prompt: What is monolithic code in software development?
options: Code written across hundreds of micro-packages
A single giant method where all logic, variables, and flows are packed together
Code that only compiles on 64-bit systems
Code written using only binary 0 and 1
questions.explanation: Monolithic code packs entire programs into one massive block (often a giant main method) without decomposition.

questions.prompt: What is 'abstraction' in the context of method usage?
options: Hiding internal implementation details so callers only need to know what inputs to give and what output to expect
Making code run without variables
Deleting comments from production source files
Writing programs without any data types
questions.explanation: Abstraction lets a developer use a method (like Math.sqrt or Arrays.sort) without needing to understand its internal algorithmic implementation.

questions.prompt: If a tax calculation formula changes from 5% to 7%, how does having a calculateTax() method help?
options: You only need to change the rate in that one method, and all callers immediately use the updated rate
The computer automatically guesses the new rate without editing code
It forces all users to reinstall Java
Methods make variables immutable so you cannot update the rate
questions.explanation: Centralizing logic in a method means maintenance is done in one place, avoiding search-and-replace bugs across the project.

questions.prompt: Where should a user-defined method be placed in a standard Java program?
options: Inside another method's curly braces
Inside the class body, outside of the main method
Outside the class completely at the top of the file
Inside an import statement
questions.explanation: In Java, standard methods are members of a class. They are defined inside the class body ({ ... }) alongside main, but not nested directly inside another method.

interviewQA.question: What is the primary motivation for decomposing monolithic code into methods?
interviewQA.expectedAnswer: The primary motivations are modularity, reusability (DRY principle), maintainability, and readability. Methods divide a large problem into smaller, cohesive units that can be understood, developed, debugged, and tested independently. If business logic changes, only one method needs updating.
keyPoints: Focus on memory lifecycle and compile-time contract enforcement.

interviewQA.question: What is the difference between a function and a method?
interviewQA.expectedAnswer: In general computer science, a function is an independent subprogram. In object-oriented languages like Java, functions do not exist in isolation at top-level scope; every subprogram is associated with a class or object and is therefore called a 'method'.
keyPoints: Focus on memory lifecycle and compile-time contract enforcement.

interviewQA.question: Can a method in Java be declared inside another method?
interviewQA.expectedAnswer: No. In standard Java, method declarations cannot be directly nested inside other methods (unlike JavaScript or Python). All methods must be declared within the body of a class or interface. However, Java does support local inner classes and lambda expressions inside methods.
keyPoints: Focus on memory lifecycle and compile-time contract enforcement.

interviewQA.question: What happens in memory when a method is called?
interviewQA.expectedAnswer: When a method is called, a new stack frame (activation record) is allocated on the Call Stack. This stack frame stores the method's parameters, return address, and local variables. When the method completes, its stack frame is popped off, freeing that memory.
keyPoints: Focus on memory lifecycle and compile-time contract enforcement.

interviewQA.question: What is meant by the 'Single Responsibility Principle' (SRP) for methods?
interviewQA.expectedAnswer: SRP states that a method should do one thing and do it well. For example, a method should calculate a value OR print a report, but not mix calculations, database writes, and UI formatting into one 300-line method. High cohesion ensures methods remain testable and reusable.
keyPoints: Focus on memory lifecycle and compile-time contract enforcement.

interviewQA.question: How does method extraction improve unit testing?
interviewQA.expectedAnswer: When logic is locked inside a 500-line main method that depends on console input and output, you cannot easily test calculations in automated test suites (like JUnit). Extracting logic into a method like 'double calculateInterest(double principal, double rate, int years)' allows unit test frameworks to pass arbitrary inputs and assert exact outputs directly.
keyPoints: Focus on memory lifecycle and compile-time contract enforcement.

interviewQA.question: What is the difference between built-in Java methods and user-defined methods?
interviewQA.expectedAnswer: Built-in methods come packaged with the Java Development Kit (JDK) standard libraries (such as Math.max(), String.toUpperCase(), or System.out.println()). User-defined methods are created by developers to fulfill domain-specific application requirements.
keyPoints: Focus on memory lifecycle and compile-time contract enforcement.

activities.title: Self-Mastery Checklist
checklist: Monolithic Code: Writing all logic in one gigantic main block leads to duplicate bugs and high cognitive load.
Methods: Named, self-contained subprograms that can be called repeatedly from anywhere in the application.
DRY Principle: Don't Repeat Yourself: centralize business rules so maintenance occurs in one single place.
Abstraction: Callers interact with what a method does without worrying about its internal algorithmic details.
Placement: Methods are declared inside the class body, outside of main(), and called using their name followed by parentheses ().
